## 09:10–10:15 · §1. String processing (65 min)

**Aim.** Every student can split, join, replace, and clean strings
using `stringr` on a realistic text sample.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 3 (`03-string-processing.qmd`).

::: {.callout-note}
## Chapter state

Ch 3 is a June draft still needing the LADAL adaptation pass before Day 2.
Students should still have readable content, but the `checkdown`
retention questions in the chapter are NOT the exercises you'll run —
those are below. Use the chapter as reference material.
:::

### 1.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- A **string** is a sequence of characters: `"hello"`, `"Blockseminar"`,
  `"A wee girl of her age, like"`. In R, you use double quotes by
  convention.
- Strings are not numbers. `"5" + "3"` is an error. If you want to add
  numbers represented as strings, you convert first with `as.numeric()`.
- Base R has string functions (`paste`, `nchar`, `strsplit`, `gsub`),
  but `stringr` is more consistent: every function starts with
  `str_`, every function takes the string as its first argument.
- Encoding: text in R is UTF-8. If you see `Mßller` instead of `Müller`
  or `â€™` instead of `'`, that's an encoding problem at import time,
  not a string problem — fix at import.

Don't get into Unicode normalisation forms (NFC/NFD). It's a rabbit hole.

### 1.2 Students try (15 min)

Prompt on screen:

> With `library(stringr)` loaded, try these in `scripts/day2.R`:
>
> ```r
> library(stringr)
>
> # A single string
> greeting <- "Welcome to the Blockseminar"
> str_length(greeting)
> str_to_lower(greeting)
> str_to_upper(greeting)
>
> # A vector of strings
> speakers <- c("John Smith", "jane DOE", " Alice Zhang ", "Mohammed-Ali Khan")
> str_length(speakers)
> str_to_title(speakers)
> str_trim(speakers)
>
> # Combining operations with the pipe
> speakers |>
>   str_trim() |>
>   str_to_title()
> ```
>
> What does `str_trim()` do that's different from `str_to_lower()`?

Walk the room briefly, but don't engage long questions — the demo
covers the main functions.

### 1.3 Demo (20 min)

Project on screen. Build up to a realistic cleaning task:

```{r demo-1-3, eval=TRUE}
library(stringr)

# A messy sample — fake transcript line
line <- "  SP01: And then she was, like, 'oh no!' You know?  "

# Clean step by step
line |> str_trim()
line |> str_trim() |> str_to_lower()

# Replace: remove the speaker tag
line |>
  str_trim() |>
  str_replace("^SP\\d+:\\s*", "")       # we'll meet \\d+ properly in §2

# Split a sentence into words
line |>
  str_trim() |>
  str_split(" ")                          # returns a list

# Split and unlist for a plain vector
line |>
  str_trim() |>
  str_split(" ") |>
  unlist()

# Detect: does a string contain something?
speakers <- c("John Smith", "Jane Doe", "Alice Zhang", "Mohammed-Ali Khan")
str_detect(speakers, "Smith")
str_detect(speakers, "-")

# Extract: pull out what matches
emails <- c(
  "contact m.schweinberger@uq.edu.au please",
  "or j.smith@lmu.de for admin",
  "no email here"
)
str_extract(emails, "[a-z.]+@[a-z.]+")    # again, pattern is §2 material
```

Talking points:

- Everything in `stringr` is **vectorised**: operations run element-wise
  on a vector of strings
- Chain operations with the pipe — reads top-to-bottom like a
  cleaning recipe
- `str_split()` returns a list because different strings can split
  into different numbers of pieces; `unlist()` or `|> purrr::flatten_chr()`
  flattens when you want one vector

## 10:30–11:55 · §2. Regular expressions (85 min)

**Aim.** Every student can read and write regexes with character
classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups, and can use them with
`stringr` functions.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 4 (`04-regular-expressions.qmd`).

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the hardest section of the course

Regex is cognitively hard. 10 of 35 students will leave this session
not fully getting it. **That's OK — tell them so, up front.** Regex is a
lifetime skill; today is the first exposure, not mastery.

Keep regex101 projected on the shared screen the whole section. Use it
for every pattern. The real-time visual match highlighting is worth
more than any explanation.
:::

### 2.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- A **regular expression** (regex, regexp) is a pattern that describes
  a set of strings. `"the"` matches the literal string "the". `"\\d+"`
  matches any sequence of one or more digits.
- Regex has special characters (**meta characters**) that mean "something
  other than themselves": `. * + ? ^ $ [ ] ( ) { } | \`. If you want to
  match these literally, escape with `\\`.
- The core building blocks:
  - **Character classes**: `[abc]` matches a, b, or c. `[a-z]` any
    lowercase. `[^a-z]` NOT lowercase.
  - **Shorthand classes**: `\\d` digit, `\\w` word character,
    `\\s` whitespace. Uppercase versions negate: `\\D`, `\\W`, `\\S`.
  - **Quantifiers**: `*` zero or more, `+` one or more, `?` zero or one,
    `{n}` exactly n, `{n,m}` between n and m.
  - **Anchors**: `^` start of string, `$` end of string, `\\b` word
    boundary.
  - **Groups**: `(...)` captures. `(a|b)` matches a or b.
- In R, you write regex as a string, so **backslashes are doubled**:
  `\\d` in R = `\d` in regex docs. This confuses everyone initially.
- Honest framing: "You will not master this today. You will see it
  used, do a few of your own, and build intuition. By your Hausarbeit
  you'll be googling specific patterns, and that's normal — I still
  do that."

Project regex101.com (switch to "ECMAScript" flavour — close enough
to R's defaults for teaching).

### 2.2 Students try (20 min)

Prompt on screen:

> With `library(stringr)` loaded, type these in `day2.R` and run each.
> For each, say out loud (to yourself) what you think the pattern matches:
>
> ```r
> library(stringr)
>
> words <- c("cat", "cats", "dog", "doggy", "123", "hello42", "hi!")
>
> str_detect(words, "cat")           # literal match
> str_detect(words, "^cat")          # starts with "cat"
> str_detect(words, "cat$")          # ends with "cat"
> str_detect(words, "\\d")           # contains a digit
> str_detect(words, "\\d+")          # contains one or more digits
> str_detect(words, "^\\d+$")        # IS entirely digits
> str_detect(words, "[aeiou]")       # contains any vowel
> str_detect(words, "^[aeiou]")      # starts with a vowel
> str_detect(words, "y$")            # ends with "y"
> str_detect(words, "s$|y$")         # ends with "s" OR "y"
> ```
>
> Which ones surprised you? Any you can't explain to yourself?

### 2.3 Demo (25 min)

Project regex101. Build patterns up live, pasting a text sample:

```
Dear Sir/Madam,
Please contact me at john.smith@uq.edu.au or j.doe@lmu.de.
Our office hours are 9:00-17:00 Monday-Friday.
We received 42 enquiries last week and 17 the week before.
Call me on +49-89-12345678.
```

On regex101, build these up one at a time, type live:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `\d+` | Any run of digits |
| `\d{2}:\d{2}` | Clock times |
| `\d{1,3}-\d{1,3}-\d{4,}` | Phone numbers |
| `\w+@\w+\.\w+` | Simple email pattern |
| `[a-z.]+@[a-z.]+\.[a-z]+` | Better email pattern |
| `[A-Z][a-z]+` | Capitalised words |
| `\b[A-Z][a-z]+\b` | Same but word-bounded |

Then switch to R and show them running against real text:

```{r demo-2-3, eval=TRUE}
# A string with mixed content
text <- "Please contact me at john.smith@uq.edu.au or j.doe@lmu.de.
We received 42 enquiries last week and 17 the week before."

# Extract all digits (returns first match per element)
str_extract(text, "\\d+")

# Extract ALL matches (returns a list)
str_extract_all(text, "\\d+")

# Flatten with unlist for a plain vector
str_extract_all(text, "\\d+") |> unlist()

# Email addresses
str_extract_all(text, "[a-z.]+@[a-z.]+\\.[a-z]+") |> unlist()

# Replace: anonymise emails
str_replace_all(text, "[a-z.]+@[a-z.]+\\.[a-z]+", "[EMAIL]")

# Count: how many digit-runs?
str_count(text, "\\d+")

# Split: on any whitespace or punctuation
str_split(text, "[\\s[:punct:]]+") |> unlist()
```

Talking points:

- The doubled backslash: `\\d` in R string = `\d` in regex
- `str_extract` gets the first match; `str_extract_all` gets all
- `[[:punct:]]`, `[[:alpha:]]`, `[[:space:]]` are POSIX character
  classes — more portable than `\\w`

## 12:55–13:35 · §3. What is text analytics + the quanteda workflow (40 min)

**Aim.** Students understand text analytics as a research methodology
(not a toolkit) and have the three core quanteda objects (corpus,
tokens, dfm) built from Alice.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 9 (`09-text-analysis.qmd`), §§9.1–9.2.

::: {.callout-note}
## §9.1 is new content you need to draft

Section 9.1 "What is text analytics?" doesn't exist yet — it was agreed
as a short new section (150–200 lines) lifted from LADAL's Part 1
tutorial (`text_analysis_intro.html`). Draft before Day 2.
:::

### 3.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points — this is the one section of today that's deliberately more
lecture than hands-on:

- **Text as data.** When you count how many times a word appears,
  compare its distribution across texts, or measure how closely two
  words co-occur, you're treating text as data. The methods come from
  corpus linguistics and NLP but the research questions are
  humanities questions.
- **Core methods, briefly:**
  - **Concordancing**: where does this word appear and in what context?
  - **Frequency analysis**: which words appear how often?
  - **Collocation**: which words co-occur more than chance?
  - **Keyword analysis**: what makes this corpus distinctive compared
    to another?
- **Research design matters.** What is your corpus? Is it
  representative of the population you want to generalise about? What
  counts as a document? These decisions are made before the code.
- **The quanteda workflow.** Three objects you'll use repeatedly:
  - `corpus()` — the document collection with metadata
  - `tokens()` — the tokenised text (list of character vectors)
  - `dfm()` — document-feature matrix (documents × word frequencies)
- Everything else is operations on these three. Learn the shape of
  this workflow once and most of corpus analysis in R is accessible.

Draw on the whiteboard: text file → corpus → tokens → dfm, with
arrows and the functions that transition between them.

### 3.2 Students try (10 min)

> Load Alice and build the three objects:
>
> ```r
> library(quanteda)
> library(dplyr)
> library(here)
>
> # Load Alice (plain text — one line per element)
> alice_raw <- readRDS(here::here("data", "alice.rda"))
>
> length(alice_raw)
> head(alice_raw, 5)
>
> # Build the corpus
> alice_corpus <- corpus(paste(alice_raw, collapse = " "))
> alice_corpus
>
> # Tokenise
> alice_tokens <- tokens(alice_corpus,
>                        remove_punct = TRUE,
>                        remove_numbers = TRUE)
>
> # Document-feature matrix
> alice_dfm <- dfm(alice_tokens)
> alice_dfm
> ```
>
> Everyone with these three objects in their environment, raise a hand.

### 3.3 Demo (15 min)

Show inspection and basic operations:

```{r demo-3-3, eval=TRUE}
# How big is each?
ndoc(alice_corpus)
sum(ntoken(alice_tokens))
nfeat(alice_dfm)

# Peek at tokens
head(alice_tokens[[1]], 20)

# Peek at the dfm (as a tiny matrix slice)
alice_dfm[1, 1:10]

# Convert to tidy data if that's more comfortable
alice_dfm |>
  quanteda::convert(to = "data.frame") |>
  dplyr::glimpse()

# Chapter-level corpus — split on CHAPTER markers
alice_chapters <- paste(alice_raw, collapse = " ") |>
  stringr::str_replace_all(
    "(CHAPTER [XVI]{1,7}\\.{0,1}) ",
    "|||\\1 "
  ) |>
  tolower() |>
  stringr::str_split("\\|\\|\\|") |>
  unlist() |>
  (\(x) x[nchar(stringr::str_trim(x)) > 0])()

length(alice_chapters)

# Rebuild corpus with chapters as separate documents
alice_corpus_ch <- corpus(alice_chapters)
ndoc(alice_corpus_ch)
```

Talking points:

- Everything downstream builds on these three objects
- Pay attention to WHAT counts as a document for your research
  question — the whole book? Each chapter? Each paragraph?
- The chapter-splitting is a nice crossover: you just used
  regex (`[XVI]{1,7}`) in a real analysis
- No exercise here — §4 is the application

## 13:35–14:35 · §4. Concordancing / KWIC (60 min)

**Aim.** Every student produces a KWIC concordance for a word in Alice,
filters it, and interprets the patterns.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 9 (`09-text-analysis.qmd`),
concordancing section.

### 4.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- **KWIC (Key Word In Context)**: display a target word in its
  context. Left context — keyword — right context. The foundational
  display of corpus linguistics.
- Before you compute frequency, run keyword analysis, or model
  collocates, you should **look** at your target in context. Many
  surprises are visible to the eye but hidden by aggregate statistics.
- `quanteda::kwic()` takes tokens (not corpus), a pattern, and a
  window size. Returns a data frame of matches.
- Pattern can be literal, glob (`walk*`), regex (`walk.*`), or
  phrase (`phrase("poor alice")`).

### 4.2 Students try (15 min)

> Use the `alice_tokens` object from §3. Try these:
>
> ```r
> # Simple word search
> kwic_alice <- kwic(alice_tokens, pattern = "alice", window = 5)
> head(kwic_alice)
>
> # How many matches?
> nrow(kwic_alice)
>
> # Try your own word
> # (pick something you'd expect to appear a lot — "rabbit", "queen", "little")
> ```

### 4.3 Demo (20 min)

Build up more sophisticated searches:

```{r demo-4-3, eval=TRUE}
# All forms of "walk" — regex pattern
kwic_walk <- kwic(alice_tokens,
                  pattern = "walk.*",
                  valuetype = "regex",
                  window = 5)

# What distinct forms came back?
unique(kwic_walk$keyword)

# Phrase search
kwic_pooralice <- kwic(alice_tokens,
                       pattern = phrase("poor alice"),
                       window = 6)

# Sorting a concordance to see patterns
# — what word comes just after "said"?
kwic_said <- kwic(alice_tokens, pattern = "said", window = 4) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::mutate(R1 = stringr::word(post, 1)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(R1)

head(kwic_said, 10)

# Count what follows "said" most often
kwic_said |>
  dplyr::count(R1, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

Talking points:

- The `valuetype` argument is the main gotcha — default is `"glob"`,
  which gives you `*` and `?` wildcards; `"regex"` gives you the full
  regex grammar you just learned
- Sorting a concordance by one position (L1, R1, R2…) is a basic but
  powerful move — reveals patterns the human eye catches that
  frequency misses
- The `R1` sorting of "said" shows dialogue attribution patterns —
  typical corpus linguistics insight

### 4.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.** For a word of your choice in Alice (something content-ful,
> not "the" or "a"):
>
> 1. Produce a KWIC concordance with a window of 5
> 2. Report how many occurrences there are
> 3. Sort by the first word to the right (R1)
> 4. Count the top 5 words that follow your target
> 5. Write a one-line interpretation: what pattern do you see?
>
> Commit your code and interpretation to `day2.R`.
>
> **Stretch:** compare the same target word in Alice vs one of Darwin,
> Melville, or Orwell (you'll need to load another text and tokenise
> it the same way).

## 14:50–15:35 · §5. Word frequency (45 min)

**Aim.** Every student builds a frequency table from a dfm, handles
stopwords, visualises top words, and compares frequency across two
corpora.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 9, word frequency section.

### 5.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- **Zipf's law.** A tiny number of words account for a huge share of
  all tokens. Function words (`the`, `and`, `of`) dominate every
  English text regardless of topic.
- **Stopwords.** The high-frequency function words you often remove
  before frequency analysis — because what you care about is content
  words. BUT: stopword removal is appropriate only when the research
  question is about content. For stylistic analysis, authorship, or
  discourse, function words are the signal, not the noise.
- `quanteda.textstats::textstat_frequency()` on a dfm gives a
  frequency table.

### 5.2 Students try (10 min)

> ```r
> library(quanteda.textstats)
>
> # Frequency table from the full dfm
> freq_all <- textstat_frequency(alice_dfm) |>
>   as.data.frame()
>
> head(freq_all, 15)
> ```
>
> What do you see at the top? Does it surprise you?

### 5.3 Demo (15 min)

```{r demo-5-3, eval=TRUE}
library(ggplot2)

# Remove stopwords — rebuild the dfm
alice_dfm_nostop <- alice_tokens |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("english")) |>
  dfm()

freq_nostop <- textstat_frequency(alice_dfm_nostop) |>
  as.data.frame()

head(freq_nostop, 15)

# Plot top 15 content words
freq_nostop |>
  head(15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(feature, frequency), y = frequency)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "15 most frequent content words in Alice",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# Dispersion — how does "queen" vary across chapters?
# (reuses the chapter-split from §3)
dispersion <- data.frame(
  chapter = seq_along(alice_chapters),
  n_queen = stringr::str_count(alice_chapters, "\\bqueen\\b"),
  n_words = stringr::str_count(alice_chapters, "\\S+")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(queen_per1k = n_queen / n_words * 1000) |>
  dplyr::filter(n_words > 50)

ggplot(dispersion, aes(x = chapter, y = queen_per1k)) +
  geom_line(colour = "tomato") +
  geom_point(colour = "tomato", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Dispersion of 'queen' across Alice's chapters",
    x = "Chapter",
    y = "Frequency per 1,000 words"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Talking points:

- Zipf's law in action — top of the list is function words
- After stopword removal, you see content: alice, said, little, queen, time
- Dispersion plots are more informative than raw frequency for most
  humanities questions ("where in the text does this appear?")

### 5.4 Exercise (10 min)

> **Task.** For Alice:

> 2. Produce a dispersion plot across chapters for ONE other content

## 15:35–16:15 · §6. Collocation and network graphs (40 min)

**Aim.** Every student extracts collocates of a target word and
visualises them as a network graph.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 9, collocation and network sections.

### 6.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- **Collocation**: words that co-occur more than chance. *Strong coffee*
  is a collocation; *powerful coffee* is not. Native speakers know
  which pairs work; collocation statistics let you detect them in a
  corpus.
- Count how often two words appear together in a window (sentence,
  N words), compute what you'd expect by chance, compare observed vs
  expected.
- Measures: Mutual Information (MI), log-likelihood (G²), Delta P,
  phi (φ). Each has biases — MI inflates for rare words, G²
  inflates for frequent ones. For teaching, phi is a reasonable
  balanced default.
- Network graphs: visualise a word and its top collocates as nodes
  connected by edges weighted by co-occurrence. Pretty, and
  surprisingly diagnostic — the semantic neighbourhood of a word is
  often visually obvious.

### 6.2 Students try (10 min)

> ```r
> # Sentence-level collocation requires sentence tokens
> library(tokenizers)
>
> alice_sentences <- paste(alice_raw, collapse = " ") |>
>   tokenize_sentences() |>
>   unlist() |>
>   stringr::str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:] ]", " ") |>
>   stringr::str_squish() |>
>   tolower() |>
>   (\(x) x[nchar(x) > 5])()
>
> length(alice_sentences)
> head(alice_sentences, 3)
> ```

### 6.3 Demo (15 min)

```{r demo-6-3, eval=TRUE}
# Feature Co-occurrence Matrix at sentence level
alice_fcm <- alice_sentences |>
  tokens() |>
  dfm() |>
  fcm(tri = FALSE)

# Top collocates of "alice" — using quanteda's built-in top-features
top_colls <- alice_fcm["alice", ] |>
  as.matrix() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("word") |>
  dplyr::rename(cooc = alice) |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(cooc)) |>
  head(20)

top_colls

# Build network for top collocates of "alice"
library(quanteda.textplots)

# Restrict the fcm to alice + its top collocates
coll_fcm <- alice_sentences |>
  tokens() |>
  dfm() |>
  dfm_select(pattern = c("alice", top_colls$word)) |>
  fcm(tri = FALSE)

# quanteda's built-in network plot
textplot_network(coll_fcm,
                 min_freq = 0.5,
                 edge_alpha = 0.5)
```

Talking points:

- The semantic neighbourhood of "alice" shows up: actions she takes
  (said, thought, went), characters she meets (queen, king, cat), her
  description (poor, little)
- `textplot_network()` is the easy path; `ggraph` gives finer control
  for publication (point students at it for the Hausarbeit)
- Collocation networks are a nice bridge from frequency to meaning

### 6.4 Exercise (if time, 5 min)

> **Task.** Pick a different target word in Alice (something interesting:
> `queen`, `rabbit`, `tea`, `like`). Build its collocation network.
>
> Save the plot and commit.
